chapter: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
title: Sherman Cook the showman, and Milt's memories of him
summary: Cook was a sharp-dressed, gold-toothed showman who fascinated Milt as a boy because he courted his aunt.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: You're right. It's amazing how a guy like Professor Cook, who didn't play anything, but he had that gift of gab... He kept a lot of musicians working, man, around Chicago...
He did. He did. He did.
He had the gift of gab.

He put on a show. He was a showman. And he was a showman on and off stage. Because when he wasn't on stage, he had something that denoted that was no working man. He had some kind of sharp costume on, and that cigar.
And the gold in his mouth.
Like... He was (?) loved Barnum. Like, you had to look at it and say... Well, he'd call you. He wasn't a braggart. Just cool. But just this... It's a great man, but he didn't have...
I mean, it was limited what you could do in the South. Limited.

He fascinated me when I was a kid, because he was coming to see my aunt, my mother's younger sister, Aunt Cissy, who we called Alberta. And we didn't have any of this; all we had was church people around there.

And he'd come around with them sharp clothes on, you know, and I was looking at him, and he had all that gold in his mouth, and he looked...you know... And he was talkin' big, you know: "I got a band that's gonna play so-and-so, and I've got some fellas there." And I'm kind of... You know, I'm interested in getting started in music anyway. He fascinated me. Sherman Cook!

[CHUCKLING] Yeah, Sherman Cook. You had them all over the country. They all knew one another. They all had been in vaudeville, and then they tried to promote. So he'd call you when you'd go to Chicago.
And you'd sit up all day. You got on the train at nine o'clock in the morning, the train pulled out, and you got to Chicago the next afternoon.
